title: Mexico's becomes Minton's with gambling
summary: Mexico's lasted for years until it became Minton's place; Minton, a union official, let young musicians work, and he added gambling where Duke lost his money.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: How long was Mexico's open? How long did it last?

Oh, for years. I was there in '27 and when I left and went on the road with Duke there for quite a while, every time I'd come back to New York he still had his little spot there until the next thing you know he had disappeared.
And what was --
Then it got to be Minton's place.
Oh. Minton's was the same place that
Yeah, yeah.
Ah.
And it got to be his place. So evidently they must have did business, Minton and Mexico.

Minton was a nice guy because he used to be in the union, you know, a big shot. And at that time you couldn't work on a regular job in New York for six months when you first joined the union. But Minton, he'd let you go. He'd say, "Go ahead, son, go and meet" -- just don't worry -- because he had that part of the city to cover, you know, for musicians. He liked us. He gave all youngsters a break. Yeah, we got along all right.
That's where Duke used to lose all his money, at Minton's.
Gambling at Minton's?
Yeah.
When Minton's first opened, was there jam sessions and music like there was at -- ?
Yeah, yeah.
In the forties there were, but -- when did it open? In the thirties?
I guess so.
But Minton, he added gambling. You see, Mexico didn't have gambling, just drinking and music. But Minton, he
got that plus gambling, see.
Uh-huh.
So it was pretty good.
